senses.def: to experience a state of great joy and gladness, often involving verbal expression and appropriate body movement
senses.comment: In Acts 2:26 it may be impossible to say ‘my tongue rejoices.’ One may, however, translate in some languages as ‘I shout because I am so happy.’

senses.def: to be distressed and troubled, with the probable implication of anguish
obscene, shameful speech involving culturally disapproved themes

senses.subdomain: Application and Removal of Liquids or Masses
senses.def: to anoint with a liquid, normally oil or perfume
pertaining to not being repentant
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘a hard and unrepentant heart.’ A more satisfactory equivalent of this expression in Romans 2:5 may be ‘but you are stubborn and refuse to repent’ or ‘… refuse to turn to God.’

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to sit up from a reclining or lying position
relief from distressful, burdensome circumstances
senses.comment: In Acts 3:20 the phrase καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως is generally regarded as a reference to the Messianic age.|In a number of languages it may be extremely difficult to speak of ‘relief coming from the Lord.’ It is easy enough to speak of animate beings ‘coming,’ but to have a state of relief ‘coming’ may be semantically impossible. However, the entire expression in Acts 3:20 may be restructured as ‘so that the Lord may cause you to have relief from trouble’ or ‘… cause you to no longer be troubled.’ For another interpretation of ἀνάψυξις in Acts 3:20, see 25.148.

senses.def: a state of cheer and encouragement after a period of having been troubled or upset
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀνάψυξις in Acts 3:20, see 22.35.

senses.def: (derivative of ἀνταποδίδωμι[a] ‘to repay,’ 57.154) that which is repaid
the recompense, whether positive or negative, which is given to someone on the basis of or in exchange for what has been done
glosses: reward for what has been done
senses.comment: In Romans 11:9 one may also justifiably translate ἀνταπόδομα as ‘punishment for what they have done,’ since the context indicates clearly the negative aspect of the recompense.

senses.def: to say that one does not know about or is in any way related to a person or event
senses.comment: In translating ἀρνέομαι[a] and ἀπαρνέομαι[a], one can often use an equivalent phrase such as ‘to say that one does not know’ or ‘to say that one has nothing to do with.’|In denying an event, as in Luke 8:45, it may be possible to translate ‘but they all said they knew nothing about it.’|It is also possible to deny having done something, and therefore one may translate the response in Luke 8:45 as ‘but they all said that they did not do it’ or ‘… that they did not touch him.’

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to refuse to give thought to or express concern for
senses.comment: There are a number of problems involved in rendering appropriately ἀρνέομαι[d] and ἀπαρνέομαι[b] as in Luke 9:23 and Mark 8:34.|In a number of languages it simply makes no sense to translate ‘to say No to oneself,’ nor is it possible in many instances to use an expression such as ‘to deny oneself,’ since it almost always implies to deny oneself something. Sometimes the meaning may be expressed in a figurative or idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to refuse to pay attention to what one’s own desires are saying’ or ‘to refuse to think about what one just wants for oneself.’ In certain instances other kinds of idioms may be employed, for example, ‘to put oneself at the end of the line’ or even ‘to say to one’s heart, Keep quiet.’

senses.def: to deny strongly, with the implication of rejection
(figurative extension of meaning of ἀποκαλύπτω ‘to uncover, to take out of hiding,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause something to be fully known
to carry something away from a point
to lead or take away from a particular point

the first or initial payment of money or assets, as a guarantee for the completion of a transaction or pledge (in the NT ἀρραβών is used only figuratively in referring to the Holy Spirit as the pledge or guarantee of the blessings promised by God)
a star or a planet
senses.comment: Since in Jude 1:13 godless people are likened to ‘wandering stars’ or ‘planets,’ it may be best to introduce this expression by a simile, for example, ‘they are like wandering stars.’ In some languages there is a serious difficulty involved in translating ἀστὴρ πλανήτης as ‘planet,’ since the planets or their courses through the heavens are regarded as beneficial. In Jude 1:13 the focal meaning is upon the heretical nature of these godless persons who do not keep on the right course. It may therefore be necessary to translate ἀστέρες πλανῆται in Jude 1:13 as ‘stars that do not stay where they should stay’ or ‘… do not remain in their right places.’ See also 15.26.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: morning star) a planet which is conspicuous in the morning sky (usually either Venus or Mars)
glosses: bright star in the morning sky
senses.comment: In Revelation 2:28 the singular pronoun αὐτῷ refers to any and all of the persons in Thyatira, and therefore it is usually best rendered as plural. A literal rendering of Revelation 2:28 may be confusing, since it would suggest that God would be handing over the morning star to persons in Thyatira. A more satisfactory rendering may be ‘I will cause the morning star to shine upon them’ or possibly ‘I will bring light into their hearts.’

The term ἀφεδρών occurs only in Matthew 15:17 and Mark 7:19 and may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘place of defecation.’ In some languages, however, a reference to a toilet may seem inappropriate for the Scriptures, and it is possible to translate a passage such as Matthew 15:17 as ‘goes into the stomach and then passes on out.’ The meaning is thus clear without a specific reference to a latrine or toilet.

senses.def: one of the twelve apostles

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: a diminutive derivative of βιβλίον[a], thus, a scroll of small size

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: one who tans hides to make leather
to come into existence
to possess certain characteristics, with the implication of their having been acquired
to come to acquire or experience a state
senses.comment: In some languages there is no convenient lexical item meaning simply ‘to become,’ but in all instances there are certain paraphrastic expressions which may be employed, for example, ‘to arrive at being’ or ‘to cease being one thing and be another’ or ‘to change to be.’ One must, however, beware in the case of John 1:14 not to employ some expression which would suggest that Christ had lost his divine nature in becoming a person or that he only appeared to be human (docetism).

senses.def: to happen, with the implication that what happens is different from a previous state
to make a change of location in space (a highly generic meaning)
senses.comment: Though the meaning of γίνομαι is often given as ‘to become,’ it is clear that in contexts such as Acts 25:15 and Acts 27:7 it would be impossible to render γίνομαι by traditional expressions such as ‘to become.’ In these contexts movement is clearly indicated, and therefore one must frequently employ an expression such as ‘to come to,’ ‘to arrive at,’ or even ‘to travel to.’

senses.def: to belong to someone
to exist and to conduct oneself, with the particular manner specified by the context
to be in a place, with the possible implication of having come to be in such a place
to come to be in a place
a marker of new information, either concerning participants in an episode or concerning the episode itself (occurring normally in the formulas ἐγένετο δέ or καὶ ἐγένετο
senses.comment: Often left untranslated.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to become to a man) to become married to a man
(an idiom, literally: to become of a mind) to make up one’s mind, with emphasis upon the process of coming to such a decision
to pay out money (or other assets) as a means of obtaining benefits or in payment for benefits
senses.comment: For another interpretation of δαπανάω in 2 Corinthians 12:15, see δαπανάω[c] 42.27.

senses.def: to spend completely, with the implication of uselessly, and therefore, to waste
senses.comment: In some languages ‘to waste’ may be expressed as ‘to use up and to get no benefit’ or ‘to have, but for no purpose.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of δαπανάω[a] ‘‘to spend,’ 57.146) to exert great effort in doing something
senses.comment: It is possible, however, that δαπανάω in 2 Corinthians 12:15 should be understood in the literal sense and hence rendered ‘I will be glad to spend all I have on your behalf’ (see δαπανάω[a] 57.146).

senses.def: a marker of somewhat greater emphasis (in comparison with μέν[b], γέ, and δή, 91.6)
to extort money by force or threat of violence
to punish, on the basis of what is rightly deserved
(a figurative extension of meaning of δίκη ‘justice,’ not occurring in the NT) a goddess who personifies justice in seeking out and punishing the guilty
senses.comment: The expression ‘the goddess Justice’ may be relatively meaningless if translated literally. It may therefore be necessary to say ‘the goddess that demands justice’ or ‘the goddess that makes people suffer for the evil they have done’ or ‘the goddess that punishes people because of their bad deeds.’

senses.def: the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I who was married to Felix the procurator
to classify by judging something to be in a particular category or class
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 10:12 there is evidently a play on the meanings of ἐγκρῖναι and συγκρῖναι (see συγκρίνω[a], 64.6).

senses.def: to throw out of an area or object
senses.comment: It may be that ἐκβάλλω in Matthew 21:39 is a type of hyperbole for causing to go out, but at the same time it is possible that the term ἐκβάλλω is to be understood in a literal sense.

senses.def: to cause to go out or leave, often, but not always, involving force
senses.comment: In referring to exorcism of evil spirits, it may be necessary in some languages to use figurative expressions, for example, ‘to pull out,’ ‘to cause to to dismount,’ or ‘to cause one’s heart to return.’

senses.def: to send out or away from, presumably for some purpose
to lead or bring out of a structure or area
to cause a demon to no longer possess or control a person
senses.comment: The process of exorcism is expressed in different languages in a number of diverse ways, for example, ‘to make leave,’ ‘to chase away,’ ‘to force to run,’ ‘to destroy,’ ‘to overpower,’ or ‘to kill.’

senses.def: to cause a significant change of state by decisive action
senses.comment: In some languages, however, it may be extremely difficult to speak of ‘justice prevailing.’ The closest equivalent may be ‘until he causes all people to be treated justly’ or ‘until authorities treat all people in a just manner.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to throw out the name) to insult or slander, with a possible implication of a kind of psychological ostracism
to move out of an enclosed or well-defined two or three-dimensional area
senses.comment: In some contexts one may interpret occurrences of ἐκπορεύομαι as being used figuratively or as part of an idiomatic phrase, but ἐκπορεύομαι also implies some type of movement out from a defined or enclosed area. Note, for example, the occurrences of ἐκπορεύομαι in the following contexts: τὸ ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τοῦτο κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ‘that which comes from a man’s mouth causes him to be defiled’ Matthew 15:11; ἐξεπορεύετο ἦχος περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς πάντα τόπον τῆς περιχώρου ‘the report about him went out into all parts of the surrounding region’ Luke 4:37; τά τε πνεύματα τὰ πονηρὰ ἐκπορεύεσθαι ‘the evil spirits would go out of them’ Acts 19:12. In a number of languages, however, it may be necessary to translate the meaning of ἐκπορεύομαι in quite different ways. For example, in Matthew 15:11 it may be necessary to translate ‘that which a man says causes him to be defiled,’ and in Luke 4:37 it may be necessary to translate ‘more and more people in all parts of the surrounding region heard about Jesus,’ and for Acts 19:12 it may be necessary to say ‘the evil spirits would no longer ride them’ or ‘… control them.’

senses.def: (idiom, literally: to go in and to go out) to live or to conduct oneself in relationship to some community or group
senses.comment: The semantic focus of these idioms, especially in Acts 1:21 and Acts 9:28, appears to be the manner in which a person conducts himself in relationship to others, but it is possible to imply a certain amount of movement. For example, in Acts 1:21 it is possible to translate ‘during the whole time the Lord Jesus travelled about with us,’ and in Acts 9:28 one could translate ‘Paul stayed with them and went about in Jerusalem.’

senses.def: to pull or drag, requiring force because of the inertia of the object being dragged
to drag or pull by physical force, often implying resistance
eleventh in a series involving either time, space, or set
a dream as a means of communication
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘dream’ depending upon the nature of the dream. A frightening dream without special significance or a dream with erotic implications may be referred to by terms which are quite different from a term referring to a dream which carries important meaning, in other words, a dream which constitutes a type of vision or symbol of some reality.

senses.def: to announce with certainty as to what one will do
to announce something openly and emphatically
to cause to be seen
to demonstrate that something is true
to sow in addition to a previous sowing

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the curly hair that forms the fleece of sheep
senses.comment: ἔριον in Revelation 1:14 and Hebrews 9:19 may also mean unspun wool; hence ἔριον as ‘processed wool’ has been classified as an artifact (6.171).

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: the processed hair of sheep
senses.comment: See also ἔριον[a] in 8.15.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: pertaining to being a favorable occasion for some event
to move toward and to arrive at a point
the state of being somewhere between life and death
senses.comment: One may render ‘half dead’ as ‘almost dead’ or ‘about to die.’

senses.def: (derivative of θεός[a] ‘God,’ 12.1) the nature or state of being God
senses.comment: The expression ‘divine nature’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘just what God is like’ or ‘how God is’ or ‘what God is.’ In Romans 1:20 ‘deity’ may sometimes be expressed as ‘the fact that he is God’ or ‘… is truly God.’|In 2 Peter 1:4 ‘to share in the very being of God,’ one may speak of ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to become in a measure like God.’ It is important, of course, to avoid the implication that people can become completely God.

senses.def: a piece of armor covering the chest to protect it against blows and arrows

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the portion of the upper trunk covered by the breastplate
senses.comment: Note, however, that in Revelation 9:9 it is possible to understand the first occurrence of θώραξ in the sense of ‘breastplate,’ the meaning which it normally has in other biblical contexts (for example, Ephesians 6:14 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8). The passage could then be translated as ‘their breastplates were iron breastplates’ (see 6.39).

senses.def: (derivative of Ἰουδαῖος ‘a Jew,’ 93.172) pertaining to the Jewish nation
to cause something to become clean
to cleanse from ritual contamination or impurity
senses.comment: The set of terms having the stem καθαρ appears to focus upon the elimination of ritual impurities. From an anthropological standpoint, this means the elimination of ritual contamination, or, in other words, negative taboo. This series of terms with the stem καθαρ appears to contrast with ἁγνίζω[a] and ἁγνισμός[a], ἁγιασμός[b], and ἅγιος[b] (53.44, 53.45, 53.46) focus upon a positive state of consecration and dedication to God and may be regarded as reflecting the acquisition of so-called positive taboo, that is to say, a state of holiness.|In Acts 10:15 the cleansing obviously involves not physical cleansing, but ritual cleansing, that is to say, the elimination of so-called negative taboo or ritual defilement.|ἐκαθαρίσθη αὐτοῦ ἡ λέπρα ‘his leprosy was cleansed’ Matthew 8:3: The cleansing or healing of leprosy involved religious, physiological, and sociological implications. Since leprosy was regarded as a defilement and hence made a person ritually unacceptable, it also meant excommunication from normal social life. The removal of leprosy was regarded as an important religious matter, and the healing had to be verified by the priests before an individual was regarded as ritually cleansed. In a number of languages, however, it is quite impossible to speak of ‘cleansing a leper,’ for this would mean only ‘giving a bath to a leper.’ Accordingly, it may be essential to say ‘to heal a leper’ or ‘to cure a leper’ or even ‘to make a person’s leprosy disappear.’ In such instances it is usually essential to have some kind of marginal note or glossary explanation so as to indicate the religious implications of leprosy and the resulting ritual defilement.

senses.def: to heal a person of a disease which has caused ceremonial uncleanness
glosses: to heal and make ritually pure
to heal and to make ritually acceptable
senses.comment: Since καθαρίζω[c] implies two changes of state, (1) the healing of a disease and (2) the making of a person ritually pure or acceptable, it may be necessary in some languages, and particularly in certain contexts, to render καθαρίζω[c] in a relatively explicit manner, namely, ‘to heal and to make ritually acceptable’ or ‘… ceremonially clean.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to close the eyes) to be unwilling to learn and to evaluate something fairly
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a problem involved in a literal rendering of ‘to close the eyes,’ since this may be understood in a strictly literal sense or as denoting death.

senses.def: pertaining to being totally without purpose
a dome-like structure made of clay, in which wood and dried grass were burned, and then after being heated, was used for baking bread
senses.comment: The function of κλίβανος may be described as ‘a place heated for baking bread,’ and it may be useful in some instances to employ a more extensive description of a κλίβανος in a glossary, but this is rarely necessary since function is far more important than form.

senses.def: to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
pertaining to a disability in one or more limbs, especially the leg or foot, often as the result of some deformity
(derivative of λειτουργέω[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.22) a person who renders special service
to cause injury or harm by maltreatment
senses.comment: It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in Acts 8:3 may mean ‘to destroy’ (see 20.31).

senses.def: to destroy or to cause the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in Acts 8:3 one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’|It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in Acts 8:3 may mean ‘to injure severely’ (see 20.24).

senses.def: to function as a more or less professional predicter of future events for the sake of a fee
senses.comment: In Acts 16:16 μαντεύομαι may often be translated as ‘for money she told people what was going to happen to them.’

senses.def: a marker of contrast, implying the validity of something irrespective of other considerations
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
glosses: on the one hand … but on the other hand

senses.def: (derivative of Μηδία ‘Media,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Media
(derivative of μορφή[a] ‘nature, character,’ 58.2) to cause something to have a certain form or nature
senses.comment: It may be possible in some languages to render Galatians 4:19 as ‘until you become like Christ was’ or ‘… like Christ is.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of νεφρός ‘kidney,’ not occurring in its literal meaning in the NT) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling
senses.comment: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον[b], κοιλία[c], and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

senses.def: a preacher of repentance who built an ark

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to taking place on the eighth in a series of days
senses.comment: Since in NT times the counting of days involved numbering both the first and the last day in a series, ὀκταήμερος may be rendered as ‘a week later’ or ‘seven days later.’ Compare ἡμέραι ὀκτώ ‘eight days’ (Luke 2:21) as being equivalent to one week; see discussion at 60.17.

senses.def: a point of time which is roughly simultaneous to or overlaps with another point in time (Luke 6:3 NA28 - apparatus)

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: the negation of extending time up to and beyond an expected point
a gathering for a happy, joyous festivity
senses.comment: For the punctuation problem in translating the total context of Hebrews 12:22, see commentaries.

senses.def: pertaining to being similar in the sense of almost equivalent to
a city in Lycia on the southwest coast of Asia Minor

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to meddling in someone else’s business
the use of magic based on superstition
to take hold of firmly and with a considerable measure of force
to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
to wash an object which is not a body or part of a body
a river or stream normally flowing throughout the year (in contrast with χείμαρρος[b] ‘winter stream,’ 1.77)
to experience superior benefit or advantage, implying some type of comparison
senses.comment: In indicating ‘a superior advantage’ it may be necessary to be quite specific about the basis for the comparison. For example, in 1 Corinthians 8:8 it may be necessary to translate as ‘if we do eat, we will be no better off than if we did not eat,’ and in Romans 3:9 one may translate ‘what then; are we decidedly better off than the others are?’

senses.def: to continue to do something with intense effort, with the possible implication of despite difficulty
to associate closely and continuously with
to serve in a close personal relationship
senses.comment: The phrase ‘his personal servants’ can be rendered as ‘those who serve just him.’|In Mark 3:9 a literal translation of the phrase ἵνα πλοιάριον προσκαρτερῇ αὐτῷ as ‘that a boat may be in personal attendance to him,’ may be rather awkward in some languages. A more natural rendering would be ‘… may wait upon him’ or ‘… may be ready at hand for him to use.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to early morning
(an idiom, literally: morning star) a planet which is conspicuous in the morning sky (usually either Venus or Mars)
glosses: bright star in the morning sky
senses.comment: In Revelation 2:28 the singular pronoun αὐτῷ refers to any and all of the persons in Thyatira, and therefore it is usually best rendered as plural. A literal rendering of Revelation 2:28 may be confusing, since it would suggest that God would be handing over the morning star to persons in Thyatira. A more satisfactory rendering may be ‘I will cause the morning star to shine upon them’ or possibly ‘I will bring light into their hearts.’

senses.def: a pagan God
a promontory on the northeast corner of Crete
to keep quiet, with the implication of preserving something which is secret
that which is taken away by force, particularly in the case of war
pertaining to being narrow or restricted
one who receives a possession together with someone else
senses.comment: It is essential in rendering κληρονόμος (57.133) or συγκληρονόμος to avoid any implication of being an ‘heir’ to anyone who has died. The focus is upon receiving an unearned gift. In the biblical sense ‘heirs of God’ are those who will receive the blessings that God has for his people.

senses.def: that which constitutes an advantage
to press in hard from all sides
a building where teachers and students met for study and discussion
senses.comment: In Acts 19:9 it is better to use a translation such as ‘lecture hall’ rather than ‘school,’ since one does not wish to give the impression of the typical classroom situation characteristic of present-day schools. One may translate the relevant context of Acts 19:9 as ‘every day Paul discussed with people in the lecture hall which belonged to Tyrannus’ or ‘… in a hall where Tyrannus often taught’ or ‘… lectured.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to make perfect in the moral sense
to cause to happen for some end result
(a causative derivative of τυφλός[b] unable to understand, 32.42) to cause someone not to be able to understand
(an idiom, literally: to blind the eyes) to cause someone to no longer have the capacity for understanding
senses.comment: Though in some languages there is a close relationship between the eyes and comprehension, in many languages it is simply impossible to use the idiom ‘to blind the eyes’ in speaking of ‘causing someone not to understand.’ The problem becomes particularly difficult in speaking of ‘darkness blinding the eyes’ as in 1 John 2:11. People can understand how ‘bright light would blind the eyes,’ but it would be strange indeed to think of ‘darkness’ having such an effect. In the context of 1 John 2:11, the darkness is, of course, not literal darkness but a state of sinfulness. Therefore, in some languages it may be necessary to translate ‘their sinfulness has made it impossible for them to understand’ or ‘because they sin, they cannot understand.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have an unwarranted pride in oneself or in one’s accomplishments
(derivative of the stem φαγ- ‘to eat,’ the aorist of ἐσθίω[a], 23.1) a person who habitually eats excessively
senses.comment: A glutton is often spoken of idiomatically, for example, ‘a large belly’ or ‘a person who is only a stomach’ or ‘a professional eater.’

senses.def: readiness or desire to argue or quarrel
pertaining to that which is in accordance with the nature or character of something
senses.comment: For some languages the equivalent of ‘being in accordance with nature’ is simply ‘being as it should be’ (Romans 1:26). For 2 Peter 2:12, in place of an expression such as ‘natural creatures’ a more appropriate equivalent in some languages is simply ‘animals.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a loose outer garment worn by Roman soldiers and travellers
senses.comment: In some parts of the world the closest equivalent of χλαμύς is a poncho.

senses.def: (derivative of ψευδομαρτυρέω ‘to testify falsely,’ 33.271) one who testifies falsely
senses.comment: The focal element in the evidence provided by a ‘false witness’ is the fact that what is said is not true.|It is also possible that such a person has pretended to have been present and thus an eyewitness of an event, but that is not the focus of the meaning. In fact, a false witness may have been present but at the same time may later provide false evidence as to what took place. It is possible to render ψευδόμαρτυς in some languages as ‘one who pretends to know about something but is really lying in what he says’ or ‘one who lies about what he pretends to have seen.’
